notes:
I couldn't finish all three parts of your request. My tool budget ran out after reading three main sources: David Guzik's Enduring Word commentary, the Precept Austin chapter page (which collects MacArthur, Wiersbe, Paul Apple, Thomas Brooks and others), and Matthew Henry on Blue Letter Bible. So:

- **Part 1 (traditional reading):** covered for most verses. I found nothing specific on v. 16.
- **Part 2 (Protestant differences):** only one difference turned up, on v. 1, and I have only one side's words for it.
- **Part 3 (other views):** I read none of the Wesleyan, Lutheran, Catholic, Orthodox, modern-scholarship or prosperity/hyper-grace sites, so the notes include none of those views.

## Notes

**v. 1**
- This verse finishes the argument of 6:14–18. Separating from worldly influences comes with promises of a closer relationship with God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-7/
- **Two kinds of cleansing:** Guzik says some cleansing God alone does in us, but some he wants to do with our cooperation. "Let us cleanse ourselves" is that second kind. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-7/
- **Sins of the spirit:** Guzik says pride, legalism, self-righteousness and bitterness can be worse than obvious sins of the flesh. He also notes that Paul includes himself among those needing cleansing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-7/
- **Henry:** sins are committed with the body and with the spirit, and both must be cleansed, because God is to be glorified in body and soul. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_007.cfm
- **Precept Austin:** says the verse really belongs with chapter 6 and the chapter break is poorly placed. It sees two sides of sanctification here (cleansing, and perfecting holiness), driven by God's promises and by a reverent, childlike fear of God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-7-commentary
- **Spurgeon (quoted there):** the fear of God drives out the fear of man and the love of sin. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2corinthians_71
- **The one Protestant difference I found ("perfecting holiness"):**
  - Precept Austin: there is no "graduation" from holiness in this life, and the verse refutes so-called "entire sanctification" (a Wesleyan/Holiness teaching). https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-7-commentary
  - Guzik: Paul does not mean sinless perfection. "Perfecting" means complete or whole holiness. He quotes Spurgeon mocking a man who claimed six sinless years. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-7/
  - Henry: we should aim at sinless perfection, though we will always fall short of it in this world. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_007.cfm
  - I could not read any Wesleyan source (e.g. wesley.nnu.edu) for that tradition's own side.

**v. 2**
- Paul goes back to his plea in 6:11–13. The Corinthians' problem with him was a heart problem, not a lack of information. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-7/
- Paul handled a large sum of money for the Judean collection, which helps explain "defrauded no one." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-7/
- Wiersbe takes the denials as aimed at the false teachers who had accused Paul. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-7-commentary
- Henry: "corrupted no one" means not by false teaching or flattery. He compares Samuel's appeal in 1 Samuel 12. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_007.cfm

**v. 3**
- Paul wants to restore fellowship, not condemn. Guzik: you can confront without condemning. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-7/
- Henry: Paul could gladly have lived and died at Corinth if his wider work had allowed it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_007.cfm

**v. 4**
- Paul was bold in rebuking them and equally bold in boasting about them. "Exceedingly joyful" means joy beyond expression. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-7/
- Guzik: God wants more than a stoic "stiff upper lip" in trials. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-7/
- Paul Apple sees three themes here: confidence, comfort and joy. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-7-commentary

**v. 5**
- The story picks up from 2:13. Some call 2:14–7:4 one long digression. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-7/
- "Outside": conflict with enemies of the gospel and worldly Christians. "Inside": the stress of ministry. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-7/
- Henry: Paul could not rest until he heard how Corinth had handled the incestuous man. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_007.cfm

**v. 6**
- God comforted Paul through people. Guzik warns that turning away from people can mean turning away from God's comfort. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-7/
- Henry: look past the human means to God, the source of all comfort. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_007.cfm

**v. 7**
- The Corinthians' longing, mourning and zeal showed God was at work in them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-7/
- The verb tense suggests Titus kept passing on the good news. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-7-commentary
- Henry: seeing Titus was a comfort, but his news was the greater one. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_007.cfm

**v. 8 — which letter? (sources disagree)**
- Guzik: probably not 1 Corinthians but a "severe letter" written between the two. He reconstructs the sequence: a painful visit, then the letter sent with Titus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-7/
- Henry: links it to Paul's "former epistle" and the incestuous-man case of 1 Corinthians. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_007.cfm
- Guzik on "I did regret it": Paul disliked confronting them at the time, but was glad of the result. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-7/

**v. 9**
- Sorrow and repentance are different. Sorrow is a feeling; repentance changes the mind and the life. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-7/
- Paul grieved them "in a godly manner": with truth, without manipulation, so the relationship did not suffer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-7/
- Precept Austin: this was the kind of sorrow God wanted. The Spirit used the letter to convict them. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-7-commentary

**v. 10**
- Godly sorrow leads to salvation and a new life. Worldly sorrow only regrets consequences and leads to death. True repentance does not mean never sinning again. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-7-commentary
- Peter and Judas: both were sorry, but only Peter repented. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-7/
- Henry: godly sorrow is not repentance itself but prepares the way for it. Judas-like sorrow is fatal, and true penitents never regret having repented. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_007.cfm
- **A Protestant claim about Catholic teaching:** an older Protestant writer quoted on Precept Austin says Roman Catholics make repentance something that earns pardon. He insists only Christ's blood removes guilt and warns against "idolizing" repentance. I did not read any Catholic source to check how Catholics state their own view. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-7-commentary

**v. 11**
- Precept Austin calls this the fullest list of the marks of repentance in Scripture. MacArthur: their earnestness ended their indifference to Paul and their complacency about sin. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-7-commentary
- **"Fear":** Guzik takes it as fear of sin and of one's own weakness rather than fear of God. Precept Austin's editor thinks the two are connected. Henry includes reverence for God, watchfulness and distrust of oneself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-7/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-7-commentary ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_007.cfm
- **"Vindication":** Paul Apple says the church is the right place for discipline, not personal revenge. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-7-commentary
- **"Innocent in this matter":** Barber says the church's guilt lay in staying silent while slander against Paul spread. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-7-commentary-wayne-barber

**v. 12**
- William MacDonald warns against being dogmatic. It is unclear which letter is meant, who did the wrong, and who was wronged. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-7-commentary
- Henry: the wrongdoer was the incestuous man and the one wronged was his father. Paul's main concern was the whole church. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_007.cfm
- Guzik: Paul tactfully does not reopen the affair, and he wrote to show his care for them, not to take sides. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-7/

**v. 13**
- Paul, Titus and the Corinthians all rejoiced, as heaven rejoices over one sinner who repents. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_007.cfm

**v. 14**
- Paul had hopefully boasted to Titus that the Corinthians would respond well. Titus was probably unsure, but the boast proved true. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-7/

**v. 15**
- Their obedience was a further sign that their repentance was real. "Fear and trembling" means humble respect for Titus, not cringing. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-7-commentary
- Titus now loves them more than ever. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-7/

**v. 16** — nothing specific found.

**Still to research:** Wesley's notes and a Wesleyan view of v. 1; Lutheran writing on contrition and repentance (v. 10); Catholic and Orthodox readings of v. 10; NET Bible notes; Gill, Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary on biblehub or studylight; and any prosperity or hyper-grace teaching on repentance.
